title: Tell the beloved friend
hook: the Tenth Guru's song in the wilderness after Chamkaur: tell the beloved friend the state of his disciples (Dasam, Khayal Patshahi 10)

segments.voice: Yesterday, I never knew what You did, and your line: you made me worthy. Did you thank someone for help they'd forgotten giving? Today, a song from the hardest night of the Tenth Guru's life. Day six hundred seventy-one.

December, 1704. A mud fortress at Chamkaur in Punjab, surrounded by a much larger army. Inside, Guru Gobind Singh and a small band of Sikhs. By the end of the fighting, his two elder sons, Ajit Singh and Jujhar Singh, are dead, along with most of his companions. At the Sikhs' insistence, the Guru leaves in the dark. Sikh tradition remembers him alone in the forest near Machhiwara, on the cold ground, his clothes torn. And there, it says, he sang. Today: tell the beloved friend.
screen: `CHAMKAUR, DECEMBER 1704.` → `TWO SONS FALLEN.` → `ALONE IN THE FOREST, HE SINGS.`

segments.voice: The song is called a khayal, and it's in the Dasam Granth, the collection of writings associated with the Tenth Guru. Most of that collection is in Braj, an old Hindi literary language. This song is in Punjabi, simple and close. It begins: mitra piaare noo, haal mureedaan daa kahinaa. In paraphrase: go, tell the beloved Friend the state of His disciples. Without You, soft quilts are like sickness, and living in comfortable houses is like living with snakes. The water jug is like a spike, the cup like a dagger. And then: the Friend's straw bed is dearer to me than living in grand furnaces. Who's the Friend? God. A disciple, a mureed, is sending word to the Beloved by any messenger who'll go. The striking thing is what's not in it. There's no complaint about the enemy, no counting of losses, no call for revenge. A father who has just lost two sons speaks only of being apart from God, and of preferring the hardest ground with God to every comfort without Him. Historians debate when the khayal was written, and the tradition that places it at Machhiwara is just that, a tradition. But for Sikhs, that setting is how the song is heard. Today it's sung slowly and softly, often at night, and many Sikhs say it's the most tender thing they know from a Guru whose life was full of steel. Grief, here, isn't hidden. It's sent, as a message, to the Friend.
screen: `A KHAYAL IN PUNJABI.` · `GO, TELL THE BELOVED FRIEND.` · `COMFORT WITHOUT HIM IS SICKNESS.` · `GRIEF SENT AS A MESSAGE.` · then, large: `TELL THE FRIEND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: send word to a friend. Sit, and think of someone you haven't told how things really are with you. Picture what you'd say, plainly, without dressing it up. Then, if it feels right, write them a short message after the bell: a few true lines. If you pray, you can tell God the same thing in your own words first, or say Waheguru and let that be the message. The bell holds the time.
Tell the beloved friend. Guru Gobind Singh's khayal, remembered as sung in the forest after Chamkaur: tell the Friend His disciples' state; the Friend's straw bed is better than any palace.
Your line: tell the friend. Today, send one honest message to someone who'd want to know how you really are. Day six hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing mitra piaare noo softly in kirtan, and many remember it in December, during the weeks that recall Chamkaur and the martyrdom of the Guru's sons.
